transcript.text: Tired of feeling overlooked by elected officials and like our democracy doesn't work for us? The Voter Choice Act can help states and cities that want to improve their elections with ranked choice voting. Voters are hungry for election reform, and ranked choice voting is a simple change with a big impact. Instead of choosing one candidate when you vote, you can rank the candidates in order of Preference. If your first choice can't win, your vote counts for a backup choice. That means you can vote honestly instead of just for the lesser of two evils, and more candidates can run without fear of playing spoiler. Candidates need a majority of votes to win, not just support from a narrow base. So they're rewarded for running more positive issue focused campaigns. can't afford to alienate voters who are ranking someone else first. Taxpayers also benefit. Most cities save money with ranked choice voting because they use it to replace costly runoffs or two round elections. Ranked choice voting has been successfully adopted in roughly 50 cities, counties, and states across the country, and the Voter Choice Act would help even more places adopt it. The bill establishes a grant program providing matching funds that would cover up to half the cost of cities or states switching to ranked choice voting. Things like upgrading outdated election equipment or voter education offers. Polling shows that wherever ranked choice voting is used, voters like it and find it easy. Want to bring ranked choice voting to your city or state? Ask Congress to support the Voter Choice Act today at fairvote.org/BCA.

transcript.text: Wisconsin held its primary elections this week and the most competitive race was the Democratic primary for governor. David Crowley, a county executive, ultimately beat DSA associated Francesca Hong. A lot of people are talking about what this means for the left versus center of the Democratic Party or what the polls got wrong. Hong was heavily favored to win, but we should be talking about our antiquated choose one voting system and how it really didn't hold up in this race. There are a few things here, so stay with me. Crowley won 39.8% of the vote to Hong's 39.3%, a margin of about 4000 votes. First, that means about 60% of Democratic primary voters actually voted for someone other than the eventual nominee. So Crowley's heading into a competitive general election in very purple Wisconsin without majority support from his party's voters. Second, about 20% of voters actually preferred neither of the two front runners. In a race decided by 4000 votes, about 165,000 voters cast their ballot for someone else and had no say between the top two. Candidates. For those keeping track, that's about 45 times more than the margin of victory. Now, here's where it gets really crazy. Among those 165,000 voters, 68,000 cast a ballot for someone who had dropped out of the race. Now, how does that happen, you might ask. Well, Sarah Rodriguez, Mandala Barnes, and Missy Hughes all dropped out of the race after their names had already been printed on the ballot. eager voters took advantage of the opportunity to vote early or by mail, send in their ballots, and are making their voices heard, and then their voices just don't count at all. Now, imagine if 68,000 votes got lost in the mail or were thrown out on election day for some bureaucratic reason. We consider that a big problem, especially when the margin of victory was only about 4000 votes. And by the way, this happens all the time. Including in Wisconsin. In their 2022 Democratic Senate primary, 19% of the vote went to withdrawn candidates. In the 2020 Democratic presidential primary in Wisconsin, it was about 5%, still representing tens of thousands of voters. Now, there's a solution to this problem, and it's called ranked choice voting. With ranked choice voting, voters rank candidates in order of preference, and a candidate needs a majority of votes to win. If your favorite candidate drops out or simply can't win, your vote can count for your next choice. That means voters can still meaningfully weigh in on the contest between front runners, regardless of who their first choice is or was, and the eventual nominee can head into November with a stronger mandate from their party's. Voters ranked choice voting is already used in dozens of places across the United States and it's recently been gaining traction in the Midwest after several primaries have been won with less than 50% of the vote or when candidates have dropped out after thousands of voters had already cast their ballots. Learn more at fairvote.org.

transcript.text: California's race for governor could produce a strange outcome. Democrats could be shut out of the general election, even though California is a deep blue state. California uses what's called a top two primary. All candidates run on the same ballot, and the two candidates with the most votes advance to the general election regardless of their party. Top 2 primaries have been an important reform, letting every voter participate in both rounds of the election. But when many candidates from Party A run and split the vote and only a few from Party B run, then Party B can take both spots in the general election, even if most voters prefer candidates from Party A. Polling shows it's a real possibility in the governor's race. 12 Democrats are running and without a clear frontrunner, Democratic votes could be so spread between different candidates that Republicans finish 1st and 2nd in the primary. The state Democratic Party chair has even publicly urged candidates to drop out. There is a way though to give voters more choice and ensure fair representative outcomes. Ranked choice voting. California could use ranked choice voting to pick the top two candidates in the primary. Instead of splitting the vote, you'd rank your candidates in order of preference. If your first choice doesn't have a chance to win, they're eliminated and your vote counts for your next choice. Or California could do what Alaska. Does they advance to the top 4 candidates from the primary instead of just 2. They then use ranked choice voting in the general election to elect a majority winner. Voters would get more choices and parties would be less likely to get locked out. All voters should have a real say in the outcome of elections. Ranked choice voting would be a great way to build on what California's already done, delivering more choice and fair outcomes. To learn more about ranked choice voting, visit fairvote.org.

That means voters can vote honestly rather than just pick the lesser of two evils.
